book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community
title: An AI Literacy Program for the Whole Community
answer: An AI literacy program for the whole community means that students, teachers and parents each gain the understanding of AI that fits their role. Students learn how AI works, where it helps and where it fails, and how to use it responsibly at their age level, staff who use AI with students or student data are trained in the school's rules, and parents are shown what their children learn and how the school uses AI. It matters because an informed parent becomes a partner rather than a skeptic or a bystander.

sections.body: Everyone in a school community needs some grasp of AI, not only the people who choose or manage the tools. Students need to understand how AI works, where it helps, where it fails, and how to use it responsibly, at levels suited to their age. Teachers need training in the rules and practices the school has adopted, and in the pedagogical knowledge that makes those rules work in a classroom. Parents need to see what their children are learning and how the school itself uses AI. The problem this solves is a community where only a few people understand the technology while everyone else is left to guess.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For students, the school follows a grade band approach so that what is taught at each stage matches the age of the learner, and the youngest children begin with the ask then check routine. Teachers receive training that covers privacy and the habit of removing names, the rule that a human reviews AI output, the school's AI use levels, and how to check what AI produces, together with the pedagogical knowledge described in the chapter. That training is required for staff who use AI with students or with student data. Parents are brought in through parent AI nights, where they can see what their children are learning and how the school uses AI. The five questions in Figure 14.5 give parents a way to ask about the school's practices.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as resting on a systematic review of AI literacy in K through 12, which describes a growing body of work on what students should learn at each stage (Casal-Otero et al., 2023). Beyond that review, the text points to the grade band approach set out in Chapter 8 and the ask then check routine described in Chapter 5 for the youngest students, and to the parent AI nights and the five questions in Figure 14.5 from Chapter 14. The content of staff training comes from the rules and practices set out in this Volume rather than from a separate study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on who may use AI and under what conditions. Staff who use AI with students or student data must be trained, and that training carries the privacy and name removal habit, the human review rule, AI use levels, and ways to check AI output. The human review rule keeps a person answerable for what AI produces instead of letting the output stand on its own. Parents are not left outside this picture, since they are shown what their children learn and how the school uses AI, and the five questions in Figure 14.5 give them a way to ask about practice. The goal is an informed parent who is a partner, not a skeptic or a bystander.
